query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Preformed parts made from a FeCrAl alloy will resist erosion by high‐temperature liquid aluminum during the hot‐dip plating process because the alloy forms a continuous, self-healing alumina (Al2O3) scale that acts as a protective barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCrAl alloy (containing sufficient aluminum and chromium) in its as-fabricated state with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Expose the FeCrAl alloy parts to the hot-dip aluminum plating process (i.e. continuous contact with molten aluminum at approximately 660°C) for extended durations and cyclic exposures.
generation.conditions: Service in the molten aluminum bath during plating at ~660°C under standard hot-dip plating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of a dense, adherent Al2O3 layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The high Al and Cr content in the FeCrAl alloy promotes oxidation at high temperatures so that a continuous alumina scale develops. This scale is chemically stable and self-healing in the molten aluminum environment, thereby significantly reducing direct contact and subsequent erosion of the underlying metal.
generation.predicted_outcome: FeCrAl alloy parts will show lower erosion rates, less material loss, and extended service life compared to conventional steels or alloys that do not develop such a protective scale.
generation.baseline: Conventional materials (e.g., carbon steels or low-alloy steels) used in similar dipping processes exhibit rapid erosion due to unprotected contact with molten aluminum.
generation.boundary: This improved performance is expected so long as the hot-dip process conditions (temperature, exposure time, and thermal cycling) allow reliable formation and maintenance of the alumina scale; severely mechanical or thermal stresses that damage the scale could compromise protection.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the kinetics of alumina scale formation under dynamic plating conditions, the long-term adherence of the scale under cyclic thermal and mechanical loads, and any potential interaction between the forming scale and the aluminum plating chemistry.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of test samples—one made from a FeCrAl alloy and the other from a conventional steel. Subject both sets to simulated hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (immersion in molten aluminum at ~660°C for extended cycles). Assess weight loss, surface scale integrity (via SEM/EDS), surface roughness, and mechanical properties before and after exposure.
measurements: Weight loss (mg/cm²) over a set number of cycles
Surface morphology and composition of the protective oxide scale
Microhardness or other mechanical property changes post-exposure
Cycle-to-cycle consistency in scale formation and spallation events
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FeCrAl alloy samples do not exhibit significantly lower weight loss, maintain an intact and dense alumina scale, or fail to outperform the conventional steel samples under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
